title: The written part is a guide, and his horn Bessie
summary: He realised Ellington's charts were only a guide, criticizes arrangers, and describes his trombone as an extension of himself.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Music is not paper. Paper is not music. You know what the old guys used to say to me? This is a guide. And I thought ah these old guys are talking such trash, I don’t know if they really mean this is a guide. And I finally got it one day, years later, like playing with Duke or something, when I had most of the book memorized that we played. It’s a guide. The guys in the band are playing. I remember when I first got in the band like I’m looking at this and they’re playing that rhythm wrong.
That’s off of four, they’re practically on one, I should tell them.
Don’t do that, no, no, I don’t think you’re going to tell Cootie.

I realized man, as you develop, that off of four they wanted to hang a little longer. So I realized it’s a guide. Now today’s arrangers would say, you know you come and see the band a year later, “Uh fellas, that’s off of four.” And Duke’s music is like this. Other than the staff and the notes, that was it. No forte piano, sforzando, boom, boom. Once in a while a phrase marked, once in a while. But it was a guide. All of a sudden I got it. Here’s a man who had an idea of how to put some notes together to play this song. And now arrangers think they’re Gods. And I mean don’t even ask them if they meant that. Even if it’s a mistake in the copying. No, don’t ask them. “Uh I meant that note, that’s what it is.” And even when kids are learning to arrange I tell them, I say, “Look, live the music, dance with it, hold the paper in your hand, dance around. Like I haven’t gotten a computer and software yet, but I know I don’t want to write this way. I want to write with a score in my hand. You know what does it feel like? Like Roswell, is this real? And then go to the computer. It’s about life, it’s about air. So the other thing, they say the horn is an extension of yourself. You know I’m like 60 here, yeah, yeah, whatever, so I’m an old man, give me another beer man or something. I mean I wasn’t like that but you know it didn’t make any sense to me. Like it was a seed, it was years later, I started seeing my playing change and ultimately, I don’t really play jazz, I just make my sound and play music. You know if someone wants to say this is what he is doing that’s okay. And it’s like I’ve had that horn since I was in high school, a senior in high school. I pick it up. name is Bessie. It’s like my hand fits in that. It’s like another arm. It’s like another part of me that can speak. And you know these old guys that did it, that’s how they lived. Yeah certainly there were guys, you know, but guys that could play, you know Paul Gonsalves could do that? He loved playing ballads. I haven’t given you a chance to ask questions.
